questions.q: What is the key difference between a full load and an incremental load?
options: A full load extracts the entire source table every run; an incremental load extracts only rows new or changed since the last successful run
A full load only runs once per year, while an incremental load runs every second
A full load never uses staging tables, while an incremental load always does
There is no real difference — the terms describe the same pattern
questions.explain: Full load re-pulls everything on every run; incremental load is cheaper at scale because it only pulls the delta since the last run.

questions.q: What is a watermark, in the context of incremental loading?
options: A column value — usually a timestamp or increasing key — used to mark how far a previous load already got
A visible logo stamped onto every row of a warehouse table
A special index type that speeds up full loads
A constraint that prevents duplicate rows in staging
questions.explain: The watermark is compared between runs to identify which rows are new since the last successful extract.

questions.q: In the four-step watermark cycle, when should the new watermark value actually be persisted?
options: Only after the load has completed successfully
Before the extract step begins
It doesn't matter when, as long as it happens eventually
Watermarks update themselves automatically and never need persisting
questions.explain: Persisting the watermark before the load is confirmed successful risks silently losing rows a failed load never actually captured — the update belongs at the end of a successful run.

questions.q: What is a real limitation of a watermark-based incremental load?
options: It cannot detect rows that were physically deleted from the source, since a deleted row simply stops appearing
It can only be implemented in SSIS, never in any other tool
It requires the entire warehouse to be rebuilt on every run
It only works on tables with fewer than 100 rows
questions.explain: A watermark comparison only surfaces new or updated rows; detecting deletes needs a separate mechanism such as periodic full reconciliation or Change Data Capture.

questions.q: How does this lesson's watermark pattern relate to SSIS Development's Lesson 36, "Incremental Loads With SSIS"?
options: It's the same underlying design pattern, taught here independent of any specific tool, whereas Lesson 36 showed how SSIS implements it
They describe two completely unrelated concepts that happen to share a name
This lesson replaces the need to ever use SSIS for incremental loads
SSIS Development's lesson covered full loads only, never incremental ones
questions.explain: The four-step watermark cycle is what any ETL tool, including SSIS, is doing under the hood — this lesson teaches the pattern itself rather than one tool's UI for it.
